analysis.title: What are the biggest market dislocations? October 2026
key_insights: Bonds and equities are pricing different macro regimes. Rates markets price the symptoms of stress (multi-decade-high yields, wider sovereign spreads, Brent above $100/bbl) but equities, VIX and credit do not price the consequences (lower growth, higher default risk). DB says the dislocation is unlikely to persist.
Unless financial stress eases quickly (as after SVB in March 2023), DB expects risk assets to come under mounting pressure, possibly with a lag.

Last week the Franco-German 10yr spread widened 32bps, the most in Bloomberg data back to German reunification in 1990, and the Italian spread over bunds widened 23bps. The Franco-German spread is the widest since 2012.

Equities barely reacted to the sovereign stress: the STOXX 600 is within 4% of its record high and fell only 1.1% last week. Euro IG spreads rose only to 101bps by Friday, far below 2011-12, 2020 and 2022 stress levels. In those episodes contagion came with sharp risk-asset corrections.

Markets priced out rate hikes from the Fed and ECB last week, including the October decision and the path further out. DB argues above-target inflation limits how dovish central banks can be, as seen in repeated dovish repricings in 2022-23 that were each unwound.

Central banks tend to overcorrect for the last crisis, and the reaction function is already more hawkish after criticism for underestimating inflation in 2021-22. Real yields have risen but broader financial conditions have not reacted much by historic standards.

The oil futures curve still implies normalisation despite being wrong for six months: front Brent is $102/bbl, the 6-month is $90 and the 12-month is $83. The December 2026 Brent contract is near its highest level to date.

Markets price only the first-round inflation shock from the Strait of Hormuz closure, not second-round effects. DB gives five reasons the risks lean toward persistence: no obvious path to a sharp oil decline, supply shocks can linger (1973), energy inflation spreads into core, tightening acts with a lag peaking after 12 months, and unanchoring risk is higher after prolonged above-target inflation.

The S&P 500 closed within 1% of its record high last Friday while US 10yr real yields rose. The divergence has widened over the last month, and DB says this is no longer a simple strong-growth story because sovereign spreads, credit stress and oil are all signalling stress.
Past precedent (2011, March 2020, 2022) shows equity reactions can lag. In late 2021 the S&P 500 and STOXX 600 kept rising until January 2022 despite hawkish central banks.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Largest weekly widening in Bloomberg data back to 1990, signalling fiscal and contagion stress in France.
Contagion from French spread widening into Italy.
Well below 2011-12, 2020 and 2022 stress levels, so credit is not confirming the sovereign stress.
Oil remains above $100 with the Strait of Hormuz restricted.
The curve still prices a decline that has not arrived.
Backwardation implies markets expect the disruption to be temporary.
Small decline relative to the scale of sovereign spread widening.

risk_factors: Equities and credit repricing toward the stress already visible in rates
Central banks unable to turn dovish with inflation above target
Prolonged Strait of Hormuz closure and escalation after the mid-terms
Second-round inflation effects and unanchored inflation expectations
El Nino adding to food and energy price pressure
Lagged impact of monetary tightening peaking after 12 months

tension_points.bull_case: Equities and credit are calm: the S&P 500 is within 1% of its record high, the STOXX 600 within 4%, Euro IG spreads are at 101bps, and past episodes such as SVB in March 2023 passed quickly without a broad correction. Higher yields can coexist with strong growth.
tension_points.bear_case: Sovereign spreads are widening sharply, credit is under stress, oil is above $100 and investors question whether the economy can cope with more hikes. In 2011, 2020 and 2022 equities fell significantly, and the reaction can lag.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Financial stress easing rapidly, as happened after SVB's collapse in March 2023, would invalidate the bearish case.

tension_points.bull_case: Markets priced out Fed and ECB hikes after last week's contagion fears and tighter financial conditions.
tension_points.bear_case: With inflation above target, central banks cannot ride to the rescue, and past dovish repricings in 2022-23 were unwound when inflation reasserted itself.

tension_points.bull_case: The futures curve prices Brent falling from $102 to $90 in six months and $83 in twelve months, on hopes the Strait of Hormuz reopens.
tension_points.bear_case: The curve has been wrong for six months, the conflict is continuing, escalation is possible after the mid-terms, and supply shocks can linger.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A Strait of Hormuz reopening or interim deal, as in June, would support the curve.
